uncited: This family of methods accelerates NeRF training and rendering by reducing the volume of space queried by the neural network, thereby lowering memory usage and computational cost.
It addresses the bottleneck where standard NeRFs sample uniformly across a large bounding box, evaluating the MLP in empty space or on transient objects.

It sets itself apart from [Training Ray Marching and Integration](2199-training-ray-marching-and-integration.md) by modifying *where* samples are taken (spatial constraints) rather than *how* they are integrated, and from [Adaptive Ray Sampling](8870-adaptive-ray-sampling.md) by using static or pre-computed geometric priors (hulls, blocks) rather than dynamic error metrics during training.
All methods in this family restrict the domain of the radiance field query.

Instead of evaluating the neural network $\mathcal{F}_\Theta$ at arbitrary points $\mathbf{x}$ within the scene bounding box $\mathcal{B}$, they define a subset $\mathcal{S} \subset \mathcal{B}$ such that $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{S}$ is required for evaluation.
This reduces the number of forward passes through the MLP.
Define a spatial constraint (e.g., visual hull, block grid, sparse cache).
For each ray $\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}$, compute the intersection of the ray with the constraint.
Only evaluate $\mathcal{F}_\Theta(\mathbf{r}(t))$ for $t$ where $\mathbf{r}(t)$ lies within the constraint.
The concept of restricting NeRF queries to relevant volumes originated with early observations that uniform sampling wastes computation on empty space.
